extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics instructors, mathematics education researchers, and graduate students (those teaching or studying proof at tertiary level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and research-informed criteria for what tertiary-level mathematical proofs are, what students must learn to do (construct, read, check), and how instructors can teach proof and proving effectively in undergraduate and graduate mathematics courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for rigour and formal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs at the tertiary level are more formal than school proofs and require understanding and use of formal definitions and previously established theorems; they involve rigorous deductive arguments rather than informal justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tertiary students may use informal reasoning initially, but such reasoning must be formalised for assessment, theses, or publications. Instructors should emphasise transition from convincing to proving and help students automate formal-rhetorical parts so they can focus on problem-centred aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy in understanding and constructing proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must become autonomous in recognising what requires justification, selecting appropriate techniques, and producing original proofs rather than only reproducing textbook or lecture proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autonomy includes choosing which steps need proof, adapting known results, and developing flexible thinking across mathematical registers. Transition courses, peer tutors, and tasks promoting independence can help. Assessments increasingly value original student constructions and creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of formal logic (including quantifiers, implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must correctly handle logical structure: implications, quantifier order and scope, and the difference between everyday and mathematical uses of logical terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common student errors include misordering existential/universal quantifiers, failing to use an arbitrary fixed element in universal proofs, and incorrectly unpacking logical structure. Exercises mixing natural language and formal statements and emphasising pragmatic vs mathematical registers are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and using negation and proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must be able to formulate negations precisely (in the mathematical scheme of properties) and understand proofs by contradiction, including how to express negations positively to proceed with contradiction arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of natural-language schemes (opposite, possibilities) that conflict with mathematical negation. Teaching should include explicit practice in producing correct negations and structured use of contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be operable (useable in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should not merely recite definitions but make them operable — able to use them to create or reproduce formal arguments; they should be able to construct and revise definitions (zero-definitions, proof-generated definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks that require students to generate examples/non-examples and to refine tentative definitions (zero-definitions) help connect concept formation, definition construction, and proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpack theorem statements (identify hypotheses and conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: On receiving a theorem or claim, students must ascertain which are hypotheses vs conclusions and unpack definitions in the conclusion to inform a proof strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If theorems are informally stated, students should practice translating them into if-then / if-and-only-if forms; instructors can help by initially using familiar forms and teaching linguistic cues (e.g., 'whenever' implies 'if').

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify applicability of previous theorems and hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must interpret and apply relevant theorems correctly, ensuring the hypotheses are satisfied before using a theorem, and avoid wrongly applying converses or treating named theorems as vague slogans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common anti-patterns: ignoring conditions, applying converses without justification, using theorems as pat solutions. Teach substitution into statements and careful verification of conditions, especially for compound variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use a repertoire of examples, counterexamples, non-examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A rich concept image (many varied examples and near-examples) supports flexible use of concepts in proofs and in judging conjectures; one counterexample can disprove a conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage generation of examples (not only memorisation). Pedagogically useful examples are 'only just' examples; useful non-examples are 'very nearly' examples. Beware students' reluctance to generate diverse examples or tendency to re-use a single prototypical example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select helpful representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should know which symbolic or graphical representations make properties transparent (or opaque) and be able to move flexibly between representations (e.g., linear transformations vs matrices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach multiple representations and show how some make particular proofs easier or properties more visible. Point out representations that obscure key features to avoid misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish everyday and mathematical registers of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must keep everyday meanings of words separate from their precise mathematical meanings (e.g., 'limit' in everyday vs mathematical sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit comparison exercises and tasks applying logical principles to mixed natural/mathematical language help prevent mechanical memorisation of abstract formulas without broader reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate organising (global) and operative (local) dimensions of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must manage both the organising dimension (selecting global logical structure/technique such as contradiction, induction) and the operative dimension (implementing techniques, algebraic manipulations, using key theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should address both dimensions; French secondary teaching often gives autonomy mainly in operative dimension while university expects fluency in both, causing student difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automate formal-rhetorical parts to free cognitive resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should learn to automate the formal-rhetorical aspects of proofs (hypotheses, conclusion, routine logical steps) so working memory can focus on problem-centred creative parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One pedagogical approach is to have students write the formal-rhetorical scaffold first, then unpack the conclusion to reveal the real problem to be solved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand multiple functions of proof (verification, explanation, discovery, communication, systematisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs serve several functions beyond verification — they can explain, discover new results, communicate reasoning, and systematise concepts — and students should be aware of these roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching can emphasise different functions through varied tasks; for example, transparent pseudo-proofs for teaching vs full formal proofs for communication/verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle epistemological reconceptualisation of familiar notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often must reconstruct school-level concepts at tertiary level (e.g., tangents described globally in school vs local limit definition in calculus; equality via epsilon arguments in analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that force students to confront and revise naive concept images, and discuss differences between school and advanced definitions explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid linear 'top-down' proof construction myth; support iterative strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Students may believe proofs are constructed strictly linearly from hypothesis to conclusion; instead, productive proving can involve making temporary assumptions, exploring, and returning to earlier steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage flexible proving strategies, such as making provisional assumptions or working backward, and expose students to non-linear construction methods; critique rigid two-column proof norms where harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach reading and checking proofs (validation skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must learn to read proofs critically and determine whether arguments actually prove the stated theorem (proof validation), as many undergraduates cannot reliably judge correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use activities where students evaluate proofs written as texts, identify gaps or fallacies (e.g., incorrect epsilon choices), and practise explicit proof-checking heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote strategic problem-solving and persistence (avoid mimicry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing nontrivial proofs requires persistence and strategic knowledge rather than rote mimicry; textbooks/exercises that invite only similarity-based solutions foster mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include global plausible reasoning (GPR) exercises and nonroutine tasks; reduce overreliance on solved-example mimicry and teach strategies for approaching unfamiliar problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured proofs and generic proving as teaching tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured proofs (making proof structure explicit) and generic proving (exploiting a general class of examples) can improve comprehension and scaffold students' proof construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leron's structured proofs and other formats can be trialled; research suggests benefits for proof comprehension but teachers should evaluate suitability per context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design curricular and instructional supports for transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: To ease secondary-tertiary and undergraduate-graduate transitions, institutions should provide transition-to-proof courses, communities of practice, peer tutors, targeted graduate courses, and resources (videos, DVDs, written materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include one-semester beginning graduate courses that emphasise various proof kinds and extensive feedback, Moore Method variants, co-construction of proofs, and scientific debate to build enculturation and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess creativity and original proving at advanced levels
rubrics_metrics.description: At Masters and Ph.D. levels, expectations include conjecturing interesting new results and proving them; assessment emphasises originality, awareness of related literature, and potential publishability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors must scaffold students through adjustment, expertise, and articulation stages; assessments for research degrees require demonstration of original contribution and integration into wider knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use near-boundary examples for teaching (pedagogical choice of examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal examples are those that are 'only just' examples and the ideal non-examples are 'very nearly' examples to highlight the role of definitions and boundary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct class activities that require students to craft near-examples to refine definitions and to test conjectures, improving discriminative concept images.
